newsitem.title: USA: Burlington seen paying big premium for LL&E.
newsitem.headline: Burlington seen paying big premium for LL&E.

text.p: Burlington Resources Inc is paying a substantial premium for Louisiana Land & Exploration Co and should have a clear run at the company, say analysts and traders.
Burlington said on Thursday that it would issue 52.6 million of its shares to LL&E holders, which at yesterday's close was equivalent to $70 per LL&E share, or a 21 percent premium.
"It looks issue free; Burlington is paying one hell of a premium though," said one arbitrageur.
Burlington chief executive Bobby Shackouls said that he did not believe that he was overpaying.
"We see a lot of value in both of these companies which is not reflected in their share price in the market," he said in a telephone interview.

Barbis at UBS said that the deal would be neutral to cash flow in 1997 and additive in 1998 and he has raised his cash flow per share forecast for Burlinton to $6.60 from $6.35, although he cut his ratings on both companies to "hold" from "buy."

"Strategically we like the fit of the Burlington/Louisana Land merger. Burlington has long wanted international exposure and LL&E offers BR exposure to the UK North Sea, Algeria and Indonesia," he said.

Shackouls said that Burlington's low debt to capitalization ratio, 40 percent after the deal and the assumption of $500 million of LL&E debt, still left the company with considerable scope for any other acquisitions.
"We have $2.0 billion in firepower, so we could do a sizeable cash acquisition, or if we saw another LL&E, we would do another stock deal," he said.

He said that Burlington was happy operating in an environment of lower natural gas prices -- they have fallen in the second quarter from $2.44 per thousand cubic feet to $2.00 from the first -- as it works off the bottom quartile of price expectations when assessing new projects.
However, Shackouls said that he does not expect the price decline to continue.

"Although there will be some new supply into the market from Canada at the turn of the century, the U.S. has simply not been replacing its reserves," he said. ((-- David Chance New York Newsroom 212 859 1902))
